To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increased proinflammatory cytokines are expressed by the mucosal cells in the rectal biopsies of coeliac disease subjects within 4 h of gluten challenge, but that there is no parallel expansion of antigen‐responsive T cells.
the rectal mucosal expression of the proinflammatory chemokines IL‐8, monocyte chemotatic protein‐1 and IL‐1β is increased within 4 h of gluten challenge in coeliacs, but not in normal subjects.
increased expression of pro‐inflammatory cytokines occurs in coeliac disease patients within hours of rectal gluten exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the activation or re‐activation of coeliac sprue.
the pathogenesis of the inflammatory response in the gut mucosa of patients with coeliac disease and the mechanisms involved in the induction of mucosal inflammation in response to gluten challenge.
understanding how gluten triggers an inflammatory response in the intestinal mucosal tissue of individuals with celiac disease, and how that response is regulated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rectal mucosal response to gluten in coeliac patients is a complex and multi‐faceted phenomenon.

the rectal mucosal response to gluten challenge in coelic disease is a complex process involving the activation of a proinflammatory cytokin gene expression profile that precedes the activation of T cell populations.

the expression of pro‐inflammatory cytokines is up‐regulated within 2–3 h after gluten challenge and this precedes the expansion and activation of gluten‐specific T cells in the colonic lamina propria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression of pro‐inflammatory cytokine mRNA in the rectal biopsies of patients with coeliac disease was increased in the early period of gluten challenge.
gluten challenge of the rectal epithelium of celiac patients induces a local inflammatory response characterized by increased expression of pro‐inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

we have shown that the rectal mucosal response to experimental gluten challenge is characterized by early changes in proinflammatory cytokines and that this response is not accompanied by an early expansion in the T cell repertoire.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mucosal immune response to gluten in coeliac disease is characterized by a proinflammatory response that occurs before the recruitment of gluten‐specific T cells into the mucosal tissue.

the rectal mucosal response to gluten challenge in coelica disease patients can be assessed by measuring cytokine gene expression, and this approach is more sensitive and specific than the assessment of T cell receptor Vβ repertoire changes.
gluten‐induced activation of T cells in patients with coeliac disease occurs in the absence of changes in the T cell receptor repertoire.
